title: Redis Persistence: RDB, AOF & Durability
summary: A complete study series on how Redis survives restarts — RDB point-in-time snapshots, the AOF command log, fsync policies, rewrite/compaction mechanics, hybrid mode, recovery order, and the durability-vs-performance trade-offs of each.

chapters.title: Why Persistence At All
points: Redis is an in-memory store: the authoritative dataset lives in RAM, so a process exit loses everything not written to disk
Persistence = writing state to durable storage so a restart can rebuild the in-memory dataset
Three failure classes: process crash (Redis dies, OS alive), OS/host crash (page cache lost), disk failure (files lost)
Definition: durability = an acknowledged write survives a defined failure class; different policies protect against different classes
Definition: RPO (recovery point objective) = how much data you accept losing, measured in time (e.g. 1s of writes)
Definition: RTO (recovery time objective) = how long a restart takes to become serving-ready
Redis offers two mechanisms: RDB (periodic binary snapshot) and AOF (append-only command log); they can run together
Persistence is not replication: a replica protects against host loss, persistence protects against restart amnesia — you usually want both
Replication of a bug is instant; a wrong FLUSHALL propagates to replicas but an old RDB file still has the data
Cache-only deployments legitimately disable both (`save ""`, `appendonly no`) and treat Redis as rebuildable
Persistence writes are asynchronous to the command reply by default — Redis ACKs before data hits the disk platter
`INFO persistence` is the one command that reports every state discussed in this handbook: `rdb_*`, `aof_*`, `loading`, `*_last_bgsave_status`
Rule of thumb: pick RDB for backups and fast restarts, AOF for a low RPO, both for production
Common myth to kill early: 'Redis is durable because it writes an AOF' — untrue until you also state the fsync policy

chapters.title: RDB Snapshots: What & How
points: RDB = a compact binary point-in-time dump of the whole keyspace to a single file, default `dump.rdb` in `dir`
Config: `dbfilename dump.rdb` names the file, `dir /var/lib/redis` names the folder; Redis chdir()s into `dir`
`SAVE` dumps synchronously in the main thread — blocks every client, effectively never use it in production
`BGSAVE` forks a child process that writes the snapshot while the parent keeps serving commands
Automatic triggers via `save <seconds> <changes>` lines; classic defaults `save 900 1`, `save 300 10`, `save 60 10000`
`save ""` in the config disables all automatic snapshotting; `CONFIG SET save ""` does it at runtime
Snapshot is atomic on disk: child writes a temp file then `rename()`s over `dump.rdb`, so readers never see a half file
RDB file format is versioned, self-describing, includes a CRC64 checksum trailer (`rdbchecksum yes`)
`rdbcompression yes` LZF-compresses string values — cheap CPU, big file-size win; independent of `rdbchecksum`
Redis also BGSAVEs implicitly: on `SHUTDOWN` (if saves configured), on `DEBUG RELOAD`, and for a full replica sync
Read progress with `INFO persistence`: `rdb_bgsave_in_progress`, `rdb_last_save_time`, `rdb_last_bgsave_status`, `rdb_changes_since_last_save`
`LASTSAVE` returns the Unix timestamp of the last successful save — poll it to confirm a BGSAVE landed
`redis-check-rdb dump.rdb` validates a snapshot before you trust it as a backup
Backup recipe: copy the RDB file anywhere (it's a single immutable-once-renamed file) — no locking needed after rename

chapters.title: Fork, Copy-on-Write & Snapshot Cost
points: `fork()` gives the child a logical copy of the parent's memory; pages are shared and marked read-only until written
Copy-on-write (COW): when the parent mutates a shared page, the kernel copies that 4KB page — memory grows with the *write rate*, not the dataset size
Worst case a BGSAVE doubles RSS if every page is touched during the save; budget headroom accordingly
`INFO persistence` exposes the real cost: `rdb_last_cow_size` (bytes copied during last BGSAVE)
The fork call itself blocks the main thread while the kernel copies the page table — cost scales with dataset size, not writes
Rough fork latency: ~10-20 ms per GB on plain Linux/EC2; visible as a spike in `latency` monitoring
`INFO stats` `latest_fork_usec` is the exact fork stall of the last fork — alert on it
Transparent Huge Pages (THP) makes COW copy 2MB pages instead of 4KB — huge latency and memory blowup; disable it (`never`)
Redis logs the classic warning at boot when THP is on; `echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled`
`vm.overcommit_memory = 1` is required so fork() doesn't fail when RSS + potential COW exceeds RAM
If fork fails, `rdb_last_bgsave_status:err` and by default `stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes` makes Redis refuse writes with a MISCONF error
Fork is used by BGSAVE, AOF rewrite, and disk-based replica sync alike — the same COW tax applies to all three
Only one such child runs at a time; a BGSAVE requested during a rewrite is deferred (`rdb_bgsave_scheduled`)
Mitigation levers: smaller instances (shard), fewer save points, run snapshots on a replica instead of the primary

chapters.title: AOF: The Append-Only Log
points: AOF logs every write command that mutated the dataset, in Redis RESP protocol format, appended to a file
Enable with `appendonly yes`; `appendfilename "appendonly.aof"`, and since Redis 7 a directory `appenddirname "appendonlydir"`
Log is append-only: no seeks, no in-place edits, so a truncated tail is the only realistic corruption mode
Redis writes the command *after* executing it, so only successful mutations are logged — no 'replay a failed command' problem
Non-deterministic commands are rewritten before logging: `SPOP` becomes `SREM key member`, `EXPIRE` becomes `PEXPIREAT` with an absolute ms timestamp
`INCRBYFLOAT` is logged as `SET key <result>` so replay can't drift on float rounding
Recovery = Redis starts a fake client and replays the whole log command by command
Two writes per command path: `write(2)` into the OS page cache, then `fsync(2)` to force the disk — these are separate and that distinction is the whole durability story
AOF buffer is flushed to the OS once per event-loop iteration (`beforeSleep`), not once per command
`BGREWRITEAOF` compacts the log; `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100` and `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb` automate it
`INFO persistence` keys: `aof_enabled`, `aof_rewrite_in_progress`, `aof_last_bgrewrite_status`, `aof_last_write_status`, `aof_current_size`, `aof_base_size`
`redis-check-aof --fix appendonly.aof` truncates a partially written trailing command back to the last good one
`aof-load-truncated yes` (default) makes Redis tolerate that truncated tail on boot and log a warning instead of refusing to start
Turning AOF on at runtime with `CONFIG SET appendonly yes` triggers a background rewrite to create the initial base — it does not block

chapters.title: fsync Policies: The Durability Dial
points: `appendfsync` has exactly three values: `always`, `everysec` (default), `no`
`always`: fsync before replying — at most one command lost, but throughput drops to disk-fsync rate (often <10k ops/s, brutal on non-battery-backed disks)
`everysec`: a background thread fsyncs once per second — bounded loss of ~1 second of writes, near-full throughput; this is the sane production default
`no`: never fsync explicitly, leave it to the kernel (~30s dirty-page writeback on Linux) — fastest, loses up to that whole window on host crash
Critical distinction: `write()` protects against a *Redis process* crash (data sits in page cache, survives); `fsync()` protects against an *OS/host* crash
So even `appendfsync no` loses nothing if only the redis-server process is killed — the kernel still owns the buffer
`everysec` worst case is documented as up to 2 seconds, not 1: if the fsync thread is still busy the main thread delays the write by up to another second
During an AOF rewrite, fsync on the main AOF can stall on the same disk; `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes` disables fsync while a child writes — trades durability for latency during rewrites
`no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes` effectively degrades you to `appendfsync no` for the duration of the rewrite — know that before enabling it
Hardware truth: an fsync only reaches the platter if the drive's write cache is disabled or battery/capacitor-backed; consumer SSDs lie about this
Cloud network disks (EBS, PD) have fsync latency in the low milliseconds — `always` there means single-digit-thousands ops/s
Even with `always`, a single-node Redis has no cross-machine durability — a dead host with a dead disk is total loss
`WAITAOF numlocal numreplicas timeout` (Redis 7.2+) blocks until the write is fsynced locally and/or on N replicas — the real primitive for per-write durability
`WAIT numreplicas timeout` only confirms *replication*, not fsync — do not confuse the two

chapters.title: AOF Rewrite & Multi-Part AOF
points: Problem: the AOF grows forever — `INCR counter` a million times is a million log entries for one integer
Rewrite = generate the shortest command sequence that recreates the current dataset, discarding history
`BGREWRITEAOF` forks a child that walks the in-memory dataset and writes a fresh, minimal base file
Automatic trigger: rewrite when the AOF has grown `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage` (100 = doubled) over `aof_base_size`, and is at least `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size`
Pre-Redis-7 design: the parent buffered new writes in an AOF rewrite buffer, then appended that buffer to the child's file and renamed — memory-hungry and fiddly
Redis 7 multi-part AOF: an `appendonlydir/` holding one base file, one or more incr files, and a manifest (`.manifest`) file listing them
With multi-part AOF the child writes only the base; the parent keeps appending to a new incr file — no rewrite buffer, far less memory and CPU
The manifest is updated atomically at the end; old base/incr files are then deleted — a crash mid-rewrite leaves the old manifest valid
`aof-use-rdb-preamble yes` (default since 4.0) makes the rewritten base an RDB-format dump instead of RESP commands — the hybrid format
Hybrid AOF loads dramatically faster (binary base) while keeping per-command durability for the tail (incr files)
In Redis 7 hybrid the base file is literally `*.base.rdb` and the tail is `*.incr.aof`
A rewrite is another fork: same COW cost, same `latest_fork_usec` stall, and it will not run concurrently with a BGSAVE
`aof_rewrite_scheduled:1` means Redis wants to rewrite but is waiting for a running child to finish
Gotcha: setting `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0` disables automatic rewrites entirely — the log then grows unbounded until the disk fills

chapters.title: Restart & Recovery Behaviour
points: Load precedence: if `appendonly yes`, Redis loads the AOF and **ignores dump.rdb entirely**, because the AOF is the more complete record
That precedence is the #1 accidental-data-loss trap: enabling AOF on a node with a good RDB and an empty/absent AOF boots an empty dataset
Safe AOF enablement is at runtime, not in the config file: start with RDB loaded, then `CONFIG SET appendonly yes`, then persist the change to the config
During load Redis serves nothing useful: `INFO persistence` reports `loading:1` and clients get `-LOADING Redis is loading the dataset in memory`
Load progress is exposed: `loading_total_bytes`, `loading_loaded_perc`, `loading_eta_seconds`
Restart time (RTO) is roughly: RDB seconds-per-GB fast binary load; plain AOF much slower because every command is re-executed through the command dispatcher
Hybrid AOF gives near-RDB load speed plus the AOF tail — the reason it is the default base format
Corrupt RDB: Redis refuses to start and logs a checksum error; there is no partial load — restore from an older backup
Truncated AOF tail: with `aof-load-truncated yes` Redis loads what it can, warns, and continues appending
AOF corrupt in the *middle* (not the tail) makes Redis exit; fix with `redis-check-aof --fix`, which cuts the file at the bad point and loses everything after
`SHUTDOWN` performs a final blocking save if save points exist; `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE` skips it; `kill -9` skips it unconditionally
`SHUTDOWN` in Redis 7 waits for lagging replicas by default (`shutdown-timeout 10`) so failover doesn't lose acknowledged writes
`DEBUG RELOAD` saves and reloads in place — a cheap way to verify your dataset actually round-trips through the persistence format
Restore drill: stop Redis, drop the file into `dir` with correct ownership and name, start Redis — never copy a file into a *running* instance's dir and expect a reload

chapters.title: RDB vs AOF: Side by Side
points: Data loss window: RDB loses everything since the last snapshot (minutes); AOF `everysec` loses ~1s; AOF `always` loses ~one command
File size: RDB is compact binary; plain AOF is much larger than the dataset; hybrid AOF sits between
Restart speed: RDB fastest, hybrid AOF close behind, plain AOF slowest by a wide margin
Runtime overhead: RDB is zero between snapshots then a fork spike; AOF is a small constant per-write cost plus fsync
Backup ergonomics: RDB is one self-contained file you can `cp`/ship anywhere; AOF (Redis 7) is a directory of files plus a manifest that must stay consistent
Point-in-time recovery: RDB gives you hourly/daily restore points; AOF gives you 'as of the crash' only, unless you archive snapshots too
Disk I/O pattern: RDB is a big periodic sequential burst; AOF is a steady append stream plus periodic rewrite burst
Failure blast radius: a bad RDB is unusable wholesale; a damaged AOF can usually be truncated and partially salvaged
Durability against host crash: RDB weak, AOF `everysec` good, AOF `always` strongest single-node option
Both fork, so both pay COW memory and `latest_fork_usec` latency — persistence choice does not escape fork
Redis's own recommendation: run both, using RDB as the backup/DR artifact and AOF as the low-RPO recovery log
Choose RDB-only when: cache-like data, huge datasets, restart speed matters more than a few minutes of writes
Choose AOF-only when: disk space is plentiful and you want minimal loss but never take file backups (rare — you still want RDB backups)
Choose neither when Redis is a pure cache in front of a system of record and warmup is cheap

chapters.title: Gotchas & Common Mistakes
points: MISCONF error: `MISCONF Redis is configured to save RDB snapshots, but is currently not able to persist on disk` — writes are rejected because a BGSAVE failed, usually a full disk or bad `dir` permissions
The MISCONF fix is to fix the disk, not to set `stop-writes-on-bgsave-error no` — that flag just hides silent data loss
Disk space rule: a BGSAVE and an AOF rewrite each need room for a *second* full copy while the temp file is written
Enabling AOF via config file after a restart, with no existing AOF, silently starts from an empty dataset (see the load-precedence trap)
`CONFIG SET` changes are runtime-only — without `CONFIG REWRITE` or editing the file, the next restart reverts to the old persistence settings
Running `SAVE` on a large production instance blocks everything for seconds to minutes; it exists mainly for scripts and shutdown paths
Forgetting `vm.overcommit_memory=1` causes intermittent 'Can't save in background: fork: Cannot allocate memory' under load
Leaving THP enabled produces mysterious multi-hundred-millisecond latency spikes correlated with saves
Copying `dump.rdb` while a BGSAVE is mid-write is safe only because of the temp-file rename — copying the *temp* file is not
Snapshots on a primary hurt latency; move regular BGSAVEs to a replica, but remember that replica's dataset can lag
A replica by default does not persist its own view independently unless you configure it to — do not assume the replica has a usable RDB
`FLUSHALL`/`FLUSHDB` replicate and will be logged to the AOF; recovery means going to a pre-incident RDB backup, fast, before rewrite overwrites history
`no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes` quietly weakens durability exactly when rewrites happen — an unmonitored footgun
Filesystem matters: an fsync on ext4 with `data=writeback` gives weaker guarantees than `data=ordered`
Untested backups are not backups — restore into a scratch instance on a schedule and diff `DBSIZE`

chapters.title: Production Playbook & Recap
points: Baseline production config: `appendonly yes`, `appendfsync everysec`, `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes`, plus `save 900 1` / `save 300 100` for backup artifacts
Keep `stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes` so a broken disk fails loudly rather than losing data quietly
Set `dir` to a dedicated volume with 2-3x dataset headroom, owned by the redis user
Host prep checklist: THP `never`, `vm.overcommit_memory=1`, `maxmemory` well below RAM to leave COW headroom
Monitor these five: `rdb_last_bgsave_status`, `aof_last_bgrewrite_status`, `aof_last_write_status`, `latest_fork_usec`, `rdb_changes_since_last_save`
Alert if `rdb_last_save_time` is older than your RPO, or `latest_fork_usec` crosses your latency budget
Backup pipeline: BGSAVE on a replica, wait for `LASTSAVE` to advance, `redis-check-rdb`, then ship the file offsite with a timestamped name
Retention: keep hourly for a day, daily for a month — enough to recover from a logical mistake discovered late
For strict durability, combine `appendfsync everysec` with `WAITAOF 1 1 <timeout>` on critical writes rather than paying `always` globally
Durability ladder, weakest to strongest: no persistence < RDB < AOF everysec < AOF always < AOF always + replicated fsync (WAITAOF)
Redis is not a substitute for a durable system of record; treat even AOF `always` as a fast tier, not the last copy
Recap: RDB = point-in-time binary snapshot via fork, fast restart, minutes of loss
Recap: AOF = command log with a fsync dial, ~1s loss at `everysec`, compacted by forked rewrites
Recap: hybrid (RDB base + AOF tail) is the modern default and gives most of both
Recap: fork/COW is the shared tax; `write()` vs `fsync()` is the shared distinction; test your restore before you need it
